evidence_level: A for the tutoring model (unchanged); adds partner-operated and AmeriCorps randomized trials
pathway: Tutoring programs that give struggling early readers structured one-to-one or small-group practice several times a week raise scores on standardized reading tests.
model_match: Unchanged in substance: structured tutoring (scripted or curriculum-based, data-driven), one-to-one or small group, at least two to three sessions a week, during or attached to the school day, by trained paid tutors, paraprofessionals or AmeriCorps members with ongoing coaching. Named partner-operated examples with randomized evidence: Boys & Girls Clubs SPARK / Future Forward (tutoring plus family contact), Reading Corps (AmeriCorps), Education Corps, Chapter One, Sound Partners.
typical_effect: Partner and AmeriCorps trials: about 0.12 to 0.19 SD on NWEA MAP (SPARK), about 0.15 (Education Corps), 0.23 (Chapter One) on early-literacy measures; district tutoring at scale in Nashville 0.04 to 0.09 SD on reading tests; recovery-era tutoring across 8 districts about 0.2 SD. Keep planning on about 0.10 to 0.16 SD.
caveats: Most new trials are K-3 with early-literacy screeners or MAP, not the Pennsylvania test; SPARK found no attendance effect; at-scale district tutoring was smaller (0.04 to 0.09). Effects among new trials are from developer-involved or commissioned evaluations in several cases.
rationale: L-01 rests mainly on meta-analyses plus two volunteer trials. The search found several randomized trials of models that community partners themselves run (Boys & Girls Clubs SPARK in Milwaukee, Education Corps, Chapter One) and an AmeriCorps replication, all positive on standardized early reading measures, plus two at-scale studies (Nashville; 8-district recovery study) showing the smaller size the link already tells partners to plan on. This is direct support for the partner-runnable version of the model. Note the merged row S-0212 labels the program Ector County; the abstract says Metro Nashville.

evidence_level: A for the paid/AmeriCorps model; volunteer and virtual variants at reduced expected size
pathway: Same pathway; revise conditions and caveats.
model_match: Add to conditions: (1) AmeriCorps members delivering a scripted, assessment-driven protocol (Reading Corps) count as trained tutors, not as casual volunteers; (2) volunteer tutoring counts only at about 0.10 SD and only with a structured curriculum and training; (3) virtual tutoring counts only at about 0.05 to 0.08 SD.
typical_effect: Volunteer trials 0.10 to 0.13 SD (unchanged); virtual early-literacy tutoring 0.05 to 0.08 SD (0.07 to 0.12 for 1:1).
caveats: Add a Philadelphia caveat: in the District's own matched study of AARP Experience Corps (2015-16 and 2016-17), tutored third graders scored lower on AIMSweb than matched non-tutored third graders (small effect), so the national Experience Corps trial size should not be assumed for Philadelphia volunteer tutoring. Add: the volunteer-tutoring meta-analysis pooled mostly researcher measures, so its larger pooled size is not a planning number.
rationale: The volunteer condition is the one partners most often fall under. Local Philadelphia evidence points the other way from the national Experience Corps trial and should be on the link. AmeriCorps Reading Corps is neither casual volunteering nor paraprofessional tutoring; naming it avoids miscoding. Virtual tutoring is now common among partners and has its own, smaller randomized estimate.

evidence_level: Randomized nulls replicated; one positive trial of a structured curriculum
pathway: Structured after-school reading instruction and tutoring mostly did not raise reading scores; one randomized trial of a computer-plus-teacher reading curriculum after school did.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested models: after-school small-group reading tutoring with computer practice (null, Texas); intensive after-school and summer academic program with volunteer-taught ELA (null on tests at three expansion sites); READ 180 Enterprise taught after school (positive in one trial).
typical_effect: Texas after-school tutoring: no significant comprehension difference; Higher Achievement expansion: test-score impacts positive but not significant; READ 180 after school: comprehension d = 0.32, vocabulary d = 0.23 (single trial).
caveats: Add: high attrition and absenteeism undermined the Texas trial, which is itself a lesson about after-school dosage. The READ 180 trial is one site (Brockton, MA) with a commercial curriculum and teacher delivery. Keep bounding L-01 and L-08.
rationale: Two more randomized nulls (Roberts et al. 2018; Garcia et al. 2020) replicate the Black et al. 2009 and Herrera et al. 2013 nulls, so the not-recommended verdict is now well supported. The single positive READ 180 trial is worth naming so partners know which after-school reading model has any randomized support, but it is a single site and does not lift the row.

evidence_level: Matched-comparison nulls in three districts
pathway: Outside-provider tutoring under No Child Left Behind supplemental educational services did not raise state reading test scores.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: low-dose, vendor-run tutoring outside the school day that families sign up for, paid per student.
typical_effect: State reading test effects about zero (Minneapolis g = -0.04 and 0.03; Los Angeles not significant; a third large district mostly small and nonsignificant).
caveats: Quasi-experimental (matched) designs; dosage was low and variable; program era 2003-2011. Contrasts with L-01: the tutoring that works is frequent, structured and attached to the school day.
rationale: Partners that sell or run sign-up after-school tutoring will cite the tutoring meta-analyses; these nulls are the closest tests of their model on state tests and say what not to claim.

evidence_level: National randomized null (unchanged) plus recent statewide quasi-experiments: reading null to very small
pathway: General after-school centers funded by 21st Century Community Learning Centers did not raise state reading test scores in the national trial, and recent statewide matched comparisons find reading effects near zero.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: 21st Century Community Learning Centers after-school (and summer) programming as typically run, with mixed academic and enrichment time.
typical_effect: State reading tests: Texas center-level effects centered near d = -0.02 (779 centers); New Jersey PARCC/NJSLA ELA mostly null (2016-17, 2022-23); West Virginia no difference in gains; Rhode Island about 0.055 SD at 30+ days; Washington small or mixed; Indiana high-quality centers no reading effect; Louisiana positive for 30+ day attenders (2007). Attendance effects in the same reports are small and positive (Texas median d = 0.14), which belongs to the attendance screener.
caveats: Statewide reports compare participants with matched non-participants and so cannot rule out selection; positive estimates usually appear only among frequent attenders (who chose to attend). Pennsylvania's own 2023-24 state evaluation is descriptive (no comparison group) and reports little difference in reading by hours attended, and its federal improvement measure never qualifies. Center-level variation is large (Texas), so a specific center with aligned academic tutoring could differ, but that is the L-01 tutoring model, not the 21st CCLC model.
rationale: Severin expected 21st CCLC research to bear on SPOTlight. For reading (S5, S6) it does, but in the direction of the current row: across Texas, New Jersey, West Virginia, Rhode Island, Washington and Indiana, matched statewide comparisons find state reading effects of zero to about 0.05 SD, consistent with the national randomized null; the 2022-23 recovery study found after-school arms mostly null too. Adding A2.5 lets the row catch partners who report 21st CCLC participation counts. The real 21st CCLC lead is attendance (S1), outside this screener's scope; flag it to the attendance screener.

evidence_level: Suggestive: two independent randomized trials with state reading test outcomes, same direction; one is a conference abstract with high attrition
pathway: Giving each low-income child a supply of self-selected books to keep, several times a year for three or more years, raises scores on the state reading test.
model_match: Multi-year book distribution to every child in a school or grade: at least 12 self-selected or child-chosen books per child per year (or a large end-of-year selection), repeated for three to five years, in high-poverty schools. A single summer shipment or a one-time giveaway does not qualify (see PR-07). A partner coded Access to Resources (A2.3) or Home Learning Environment (F1.2) that does not run this model gets no evidence level from this link.
typical_effect: About 0.10 to 0.14 SD on the state reading test after three to five years (0.21 for the most disadvantaged students in the Florida trial). At 0.10 SD, roughly 3 to 4 more participants in 100 reach proficient at a 31 to 33 percent base rate.
caveats: Florida trial (Allington et al. 2010) used 17 schools and three years of end-of-year book fairs; Milwaukee trial (Bernie's Book Bank) is reported only in a conference abstract, with 59 percent attrition (balanced across arms). Effects are cumulative and small per year; no study tested Philadelphia. Books alone for one summer did not work in several trials.
rationale: This is the clearest low-cost, partner-runnable reading strategy the search found that was tested against the state test itself. Two independent randomized trials, in Florida and Milwaukee, with different operators (researchers; a nonprofit book bank), point the same way on state reading tests. Under the bar, one is suggestive and the second is a replication, but the abstract-only status and attrition of the second argue for "suggestive" until the full paper is checked. Directly answers the question of what hundreds of programs could do differently: book distribution and child choice of books are cheap to add.

evidence_level: Several randomized nulls at scale; positive only with teacher and parent scaffolding or in subgroups
pathway: Mailing a child a set of books for one summer, without classroom preparation and family follow-up, did not raise reading comprehension scores.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: one summer of 8 to 10 books matched to reading level mailed home, with postcards or reminder letters. The scaffolded version (end-of-year teacher lessons on reading at home, parent guidance, comprehension prompts) helped in some trials.
typical_effect: Lexile-matched mailing (NCEE trial, Texas grade 3): no impact. READS replications in North Carolina: about zero overall (g about -0.03 to 0.01). 463-classroom trial: effects only for third-grade girls. Scaffolded version (Kim & White 2008): books plus oral reading and comprehension scaffolding beat control; books only did not.
caveats: Outcomes are standardized reading tests the following fall, not the state test. Subgroup gains (Black and Latino students, students owning few books, third-grade girls) appeared in some trials but were not replicated consistently.
rationale: Book giveaways are among the most common partner activities. The evidence splits by model: single-summer mailing fails at scale (several randomized nulls), while multi-year, school-based distribution succeeded (PR-06). Listing the null keeps partners from claiming a reading-test gain for a one-time giveaway.

evidence_level: Meta-analysis and systematic review: comprehension effect about zero
pathway: Setting aside time for independent silent reading (free reading, drop-everything-and-read) does not raise reading comprehension.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: in-school independent reading time without instruction.
typical_effect: Comprehension g about -0.01 (47 studies); small gains in word recognition (0.21) and reading attitude (0.18).
caveats: School-day independent reading, not after-school; partners who run reading time can still claim reading attitude or interest (Y2.3), not test gains.
rationale: Many after-school literacy blocks are independent reading time. Two syntheses say this does not move comprehension, the skill the state ELA test measures most.

evidence_level: Randomized nulls replicated for reading; one positive quasi-experiment and one positive older trial
pathway: Voluntary summer learning programs gave small and short-lived reading effects; only students who attended a lot, a non-randomized comparison, showed lasting differences.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested models: five- to six-week academic summer programs (BELL elementary and middle school, Teach Baltimore, National Summer Learning Project districts).
typical_effect: BELL middle school (randomized): reading about 0.01 SD; Teach Baltimore (randomized, three summers): no intent-to-treat effect; BELL elementary 2005 (randomized): positive reading gain of about one month on a study test; a multi-summer California nonprofit program (quasi-experiment): modest ELA gain plus fewer absences.
caveats: The positive quasi-experiment (Pyne, Messner & Dee 2023) is a single mature program with an SEL curriculum and multi-summer dosage; its attendance result belongs to the attendance screener. Complier effects for frequent attenders are not randomized.
rationale: More randomized summer-program nulls for reading replicate the National Summer Learning Project pattern in L-07. The Pyne-Messner-Dee quasi-experiment is the strongest positive and is worth naming as the model to watch (multi-summer, SEL plus academics), but one quasi-experiment does not overturn several randomized nulls.

evidence_level: Suggestive: one strong quasi-experiment (student fixed effects) on the state ELA test, supported by an earlier matched study
pathway: Joining a competitive policy debate team, where students research, read and argue evidence every week, raises state English language arts test scores.
model_match: An interscholastic policy debate league run with schools by a community partner: weekly coached practice in research and argumentation, regular tournaments, across at least a school year, middle or high school. A partner coded Critical Thinking (Y1.7) or Communication (Y4.6) that does not run competitive debate gets no evidence level from this link.
typical_effect: About 0.13 SD on the state ELA test (Boston, student fixed effects), largest for the lowest prior achievers; no harm to math or attendance. At 0.13 SD, about 4 to 5 more debaters in 100 reach proficient at a 31 to 33 percent base rate.
caveats: Student fixed effects compare each student with themselves before and after joining, which removes stable differences but not changes that lead students to join. Single city (Boston); the Chicago study used an older matched design and ACT reading, not a state test. Keystone Literature was not tested; the high school MCAS ELA is the nearest measure.
rationale: This is the only enrichment activity in the search with a credible within-student estimate on a state ELA test, and it is partner-run (urban debate leagues). One quasi-experiment gives suggestive evidence at most; the methods reviewer should decide whether suggestive warrants recommend-with-conditions or a not-recommended row with a note.

evidence_level: Suggestive: one quasi-experiment with two methods on a grade 10 state ELA exam, supported by a grades 7-12 meta-analysis
pathway: Daily tutorials built into the school day for high school students, taught by full-time trained tutors, raise high school English exam scores.
model_match: Daily one-to-one or two-to-one tutorials during the school day (about two hours a day in the tested school), taught by full-time trained tutors (recent college graduates as fellows), in high school. Mirrors L-03 (math tutoring and Keystone Algebra I) for literature.
typical_effect: Grade 10 state ELA exam: 0.15 to 0.25 SD per year (one Boston charter school). Plan on the lower end.
caveats: One charter school with an extended day; no Keystone Literature data; the meta-analysis pools reading interventions in grades 7-12, not this model alone. Philadelphia partners rarely have this much school-day time.
rationale: S12 (Keystone Literature) has no recommended link in the map. The closest tested partner-type model is the MATCH tutorial corps (the model behind Saga in L-03), evaluated on a high school state ELA exam. Suggestive only.

evidence_level: Cluster randomized null on a state reading test; quasi-experimental null or negative; national propensity analyses null
pathway: Arts experiences, arts-integrated literacy lessons and music training did not raise reading or English test scores in the strongest studies.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested models: arts-integrated literacy curriculum with teaching artists (A4L, 32 schools); school arts lessons and arts technology (Lyceum); music and performing arts lessons (national data); high school music courses (SAT).
typical_effect: A4L: state reading test g about -0.03 to 0.05 (cluster randomized). Lyceum: no ELA difference except one cohort where comparison students scored higher. National data: no causal association with cognitive outcomes; music students' SAT advantage disappeared with controls.
caveats: One small cluster trial of drama strategies in ELA classrooms (Walker et al. 2011, 4 vs 4 schools) reported large gains in state ELA pass rates; it is unreplicated and may not account for clustering. Add S12 because the SAT and high school evidence is the nearest to Keystone Literature.
rationale: Arts partners make up a large share of the corpus. The new cluster randomized null on a state reading test (A4L) is the strongest test yet of the arts-integrated literacy model and confirms L-50. Naming the Walker trial as the lone positive keeps the row honest.

evidence_level: Two opt-in comparisons with prior-score adjustment; selection not ruled out
pathway: Students in intensive after-school orchestra programs (El Sistema style) scored slightly higher on state ELA tests than similar students, but those who join and stay may differ.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: free, multi-year, several-days-a-week ensemble music programs (OrchKids, Harmony Project).
typical_effect: Harmony Project: ELA about 0.08 SD (beta) after baseline adjustment; OrchKids: positive state test comparisons for students persisting more than one year.
caveats: Both are opt-in and the OrchKids sample is conditioned on persistence; funder-supported evaluations. Bounded by L-50.
rationale: El Sistema-style programs exist in Philadelphia and will cite these studies; they do not meet the associated bar (two adjusted longitudinal studies of the program, but persistence selection), so list them as checked and turned down.

evidence_level: Single cluster randomized trial in England; reading finding low to moderate security
pathway: An enrichment-credit program (clubs, museum and library visits, volunteering, with certificates and a graduation) gave a small reading gain in one English trial, but not for disadvantaged pupils.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Children's University, 30+ hours a year of chosen extracurricular activities with credits.
typical_effect: About 2 months additional progress in reading (low to moderate security); no additional reading progress for pupils ever eligible for free meals.
caveats: England, Key Stage 2 tests; 7 of 36 schools did not implement; volunteers only.
rationale: Closest randomized test of a general enrichment model against a national reading test. Too weak and not effective for disadvantaged pupils, so listed as not recommended.

evidence_level: School-level comparison commissioned by the program
pathway: Schools partnered with City Year AmeriCorps teams more often raised ELA proficiency rates than similar schools, in a study commissioned by City Year.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: City Year whole-school near-peer service (tutoring, attendance and behavior coaching by AmeriCorps teams).
typical_effect: Partner schools two to three times more likely to increase ELA proficiency rates; about one month of added learning (school level).
caveats: School-level, non-randomized, commissioned; schools chose to partner. City Year operates in Philadelphia and is part of Diplomas Now (L-41). Student-level effects not estimated.
rationale: City Year is a large Philadelphia partner; its main outcome study is below the bar and should be listed so the claim is not made from it.

evidence_level: No indicator outcome measured
pathway: The Free Library of Philadelphia's drop-in after-school literacy program (LEAP) was evaluated descriptively, with no school-record or state-test outcome.
model_match: Not used for credit. Model: free, voluntary drop-in literacy enrichment in library branches.
typical_effect: None on an indicator.
caveats: Absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect. A Philadelphia program that partners may cite for literacy.
rationale: Records that the search checked the Philadelphia library program and found no indicator outcome.

evidence_level: Sponsor-commissioned matched comparison in selected high-fidelity districts; district assessments
pathway: A summer reading program that coaches families to teach reading at home showed faster reading growth than non-participants in districts chosen for high fidelity.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Springboard Summer (five weeks of reading instruction plus weekly family workshops and incentives).
typical_effect: About +0.33 SD on district reading assessments (Evidence for ESSA, Promising).
caveats: Propensity score matching only; districts selected for fidelity; commissioned evaluation; not the state test. Contrasts with randomized summer nulls in L-07 and PR-09.
rationale: Springboard Collaborative started in Philadelphia, so partners will cite this. Its evidence does not meet the tested bar.

evidence_level: Randomized trials on early literacy before kindergarten or in kindergarten; no link to the grade 3 test
pathway: Weekly text messages that give parents of preschoolers short literacy activities raised early literacy skills, but no checked study follows children to the grade 3 reading test.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Ready4K-style weekly literacy texts to parents.
typical_effect: Early literacy gains in preschool and kindergarten (Evidence for ESSA mean about +0.10).
caveats: Pre-kindergarten and kindergarten outcomes only; same logic as L-35 (readiness without a grade 3 link).
rationale: Texting families is a common low-cost partner activity. The early literacy effect is real but stops short of the grade 3 indicator, so it cannot be credited toward S5.

evidence_level: Meta-analysis of mixed designs, mostly researcher measures
pathway: Older students tutoring younger students (cross-age tutoring) improves both groups' academic measures in mixed-design studies.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: cross-age peer tutoring (older youth tutor younger children).
typical_effect: Overall 0.34 (tutees 0.33, tutors 0.39), mostly on researcher-designed measures.
caveats: Designs mixed and measures mostly not standardized tests; size not a planning number. Teen-tutor programs should plan on the volunteer size in L-01 at most.
rationale: Teen tutoring is a frequent youth-program activity; the meta-analysis looks strong but does not meet the bar for state-test credit.

evidence_level: Experimental-only review null; quality-restricted meta-analysis smaller; single positive quasi-experiment
pathway: Out-of-school-time programs with academic instruction raise reading achievement a little in mixed-design reviews, but reviews limited to experiments find little or no effect.
model_match: Unchanged: not used for credit.
typical_effect: Experimental-only Campbell review: academic effects small and not significant; quality-restricted meta-analysis: effects change when lower-quality studies are dropped (record values); one propensity-matched community-provider study: moderate gain on grade 3 reading.
caveats: Add: the positive community-provider study (Baker et al. 2018) is a single quasi-experiment and does not change the tier.
rationale: Reviews restricted to stronger designs move in the direction of the current verdict, and should be on the row.
